patterns.rationale: Matches the actual BiDi directional control codepoints that every miss relies on — U+202A (LRE), U+202B (RLE), U+202C (PDF), U+202D (LRO), U+202E (RLO), U+200F (RLM), and U+2066–U+2069 (LRI, RLI, FSI, PDI). None of these characters appear in the known-good English-only corpus (deployment checklists, IR playbooks, API references). Implementation note: this must live in a non-raw Python string (or have the characters embedded literally), because `\u` escapes are not interpreted in raw strings — the final `re.compile` call should concatenate a regular string fragment `"[\u202a-\u202e\u200f\u2066-\u2069]"` alongside the existing raw-string alternations.
patterns.fp_notes: Would fire on documents legitimately containing Arabic or Hebrew text, but the known-good corpus is English-only; if the scanner is ever deployed against multilingual content, scope this to documents whose overall character distribution is LTR.

patterns.rationale: Matches the reversed `get_env()` token — `)(vne_teg` — with an optional U+200B (zero-width space) permitted between each character. This handles Miss 8's inter-character ZWS obfuscation while also catching the bare reversed form in misses 1, 2, 3, and 10. It is belt-and-suspenders against a future variant that omits BiDi markers entirely but still relies on the reversed tool name for visual deception. The string `)(vne_teg` is syntactically meaningless in LTR English and has no plausible benign occurrence. Same non-raw-string implementation note as Pattern 1 applies for the `\u200b` escape.
patterns.fp_notes: None — the character sequence is pure garbage in LTR prose and would not appear in any legitimate technical document.
